Leadership, Halakha, and Statecraft: The Activity and Rabbinic Scholarship of Rishon LeZion Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim

This survey presents the life history and scholarship of Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim, who served as Rishon LeZion and Chief Rabbi of Israel, focusing on the unique combination of rooted halakhic leadership with a broad statist conception. The text traces his path from his childhood in Baghdad until his immigration to the Land of Israel, and emphasizes his public activity in bringing hearts together among sections of the people and his steadfast defense of the honor of the Torah and Jewish sovereignty. At the center of the source stand his clear legal rulings on burning national issues, alongside the complex "brother and sister affair" that ultimately led to the termination of his tenure following political pressures. In conclusion, the work illuminates his rich Torah legacy that continues to exist through his books and the memorial institution established in his memory, expressing absolute commitment to halakha alongside love of Israel.

Leadership, Halakha, and Statecraft: The Activity and Rabbinic Scholarship of Rishon LeZion Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim

Roots in Baghdad and Immigration to the Land of Israel: The Personal and Torah Foundations

Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim was born in Baghdad on the first day of Hanukkah, 25 Kislev 5656 (December 12, 1895), to Rahamim, who was a native of Iran, and Amam.[1] Due to his birth on the Festival of Lights he was called "Nissim," and this second name became over the years his official family name.[1] Already from his early youth in Baghdad he stood out as a Torah prodigy, as a profound scholar and as an exceptional wellspring whose opinion was heard with great attention in matters of spirit and rabbinate.[2] He acquired his Torah education from the spiritual giants of Babylonian Jewry of that period, among them the kabbalist Rabbi Shimon Agassi and Rabbi Tzedakah Hutzin (the Second).[1] His Torah and scholarly connections quickly branched beyond the borders of Iraq, and he conducted extensive halakhic correspondence with the Torah luminaries in the Land of Israel and with the prominent sages of Ashkenaz and Poland.[2]

The family environment in which he grew up was saturated with Torah and public activity, but also with severe tragedies that shaped his national character. At the beginning of 1917, in the midst of World War I, his brother, Shelomo Tzion, was brutally murdered by the Ottoman authorities in Baghdad, together with eighteen other Jewish money changers who were falsely accused.[1] In memory of those murdered, Rabbi Nissim composed a special lamentation ("Kinat Baghdad"), which was customarily read for many years in the synagogues of immigrants from Babylonia in Iraq and in Israel.[1] Rabbi Nissim's other brothers were prominent Torah figures in their own right: Rabbi Yehezkel Ezra Rahamim, and Rabbi Avraham Haim Rahamim, who was a rosh yeshiva, kabbalist and the outstanding disciple of the "Ben Ish Hai" (Rabbi Yosef Haim), and even proofread his teacher's books.[1]

In the year 5680 (1919), at age twenty-four, Rabbi Nissim married Victoria.[1, 3] During these years he began to stand out as an unofficial leader of the Jewish community in Baghdad, established regulations in the local rabbinical courts and study halls, and actively assisted Jews who sought to immigrate to the Land of Israel.[3] In the year 5684 (1924), at age twenty-eight, he fulfilled his life's aspiration and immigrated to the Land together with his wife in a journey on donkeys that lasted about a month.[1, 3] The two established their home in northern Jerusalem, in an area that at that time was desolate and lacking basic infrastructure such as water, roads or sidewalks.[3] Due to economic difficulties and lack of funds to finance the building of the house, the Rabbi was forced to return to Baghdad for a brief period, but in the month of Iyyar 5685 (1925) he returned finally to Jerusalem, while firmly refusing the entreaties of the community leaders in Baghdad to return to Iraq and serve there in the rabbinate.[1, 3]

With his final settlement in Jerusalem, his home became a "house of assembly for sages" and a vibrant Torah center, to which the sages and luminaries of Israel flocked daily to study and clarify complex halakhic issues.[2, 3] Rabbi Nissim became deeply friendly with the Torah luminaries in Jerusalem, among them Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak HaKohen Kook, the elderly kabbalist Rabbi Shlomo Eliezer Alfandari and Rabbi Hizkiyahu Shabetai.[1] Alongside his enormous diligence in Torah, he engaged in commerce for his livelihood in order not to make the Torah a spade with which to dig.[1]

The Path to the Seat of Leadership and His Tenure as Rishon LeZion

Rabbi Nissim's involvement in public life in the young State of Israel increased over the years, from an aspiration to influence the spiritual character of the sovereign state. In 1951 he ran for the Second Knesset as number two on the "Emunei Yisrael" list established by the educator and author Rabbi Eliyahu Ki Tov, but the list did not succeed in passing the electoral threshold.[1] Despite this, his public standing as an independent and broad-minded Torah personality became increasingly established. In 1953, when the Rishon LeZion and Sephardic Chief Rabbi, Rabbi Ben-Zion Meir Hai Uziel, was approaching death, he turned to Rabbi Nissim with a personal request that he continue his path and accept upon himself the position of Rishon LeZion.[1]

In the year 5715 (1955) elections for the Chief Rabbinate were held. Rabbi Nissim was elected to the position of Rishon LeZion and the 37th Sephardic Chief Rabbi of Israel, after winning 42 votes in competition with the Rabbi of Tel Aviv, Rabbi Yaakov Moshe Toledano, who received 27 votes.[1] The festive coronation ceremony was held on 6 Nisan 5715.[1] With his entry into office, his intellectual independence and unique path in all areas of the institution's activity were immediately apparent.[2] He served in his exalted position for approximately 17 years, alongside his Ashkenazi colleagues – Rabbi Yitzhak Isaac HaLevi Herzog and subsequently Rabbi Isser Yehuda Unterman.[1] His leadership was characterized by a broad statist vision that aspired to bridge social and ethnic gaps, but on the other hand encountered fierce opposition from conservative haredi circles who saw him as too liberal a rabbi and worked ceaselessly to replace him.[1]

The Distinguished Disciples of Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim

Rabbi Nissim established a special study hall for training rabbis, intended to shape a new generation of spiritual leaders capable of rendering halakhic decisions based on understanding the needs of the hour and modern society.[1] This study hall produced exceptional Torah scholars who profoundly influenced the world of Torah and rabbinical courts in Israel [1]:

His Halakhic Scholarship: "Concise and Pure" and Confronting the Challenges of Jewish Sovereignty

The halakhic scholarship of Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim was characterized by clarity, directness and pursuit of clear practical resolution.[2] As a decisor, he avoided lengthy casuistry and focused on analyzing sources and formulating decisive and clear rulings, a quality defined by his contemporaries as "concise and pure" adjudication.[2] Maintaining Jewish sovereignty in the Land of Israel was perceived by him not only as a political event, but as a categorical religious transformation requiring halakhic decisors to courageously confront the public and national questions of the hour.

Two central halakhic and public decisions exemplify his special combination of Torah independence with statist vision:

Permitting Ascent to the Temple Mount: While many rabbis of the period tended to categorically prohibit any ascent whatsoever to the Temple Mount out of concern for karet, Rabbi Nissim ruled that it is permitted for Jews to ascend to certain areas of the Temple Mount, while strictly observing the required purity laws.[1] This ruling was not merely a theoretical decision, but a move intended to demonstrate and strengthen Jewish sovereignty in the place most sacred to the Jewish people immediately after its liberation in the Six-Day War.[1] He saw Jewish presence on the Mount as an essential tool for preserving national control of the site.

Insistence in the "Who is a Jew" Polemic: During the stormy public polemic surrounding amendment of the Law of Return and the definition of nationality in the population registry, Rabbi Nissim displayed uncompromising steadfastness.[1] He refused to accept compromises that would enable self-definition of nationality not conforming to the rules of halakha, and worked vigorously so that determination of a person's Jewishness would be made solely according to Torah law.[1] To this end, he mobilized broad international support through correspondence with the great rabbis of the world, and thereby contributed to fortifying the halakhic status of the Israeli identity card.[1]

During his tenure as Chief Rabbi, the State of Israel became the great Torah center of the Diaspora, and Rabbi Nissim was required to respond to thousands of complex halakhic questions addressed to him from all over the world.[2] His rulings, which were distinguished by concise and clear language, dealt with all areas of life—from individual questions to questions of state governance.[1, 2]

Public Leadership: Breaking Down Barriers and Preserving the Honor of the Nation

Rabbi Nissim's central goal as Rishon LeZion was to unite the different tribes that comprised the young Israeli society.[3] In his installation address he declared that his primary task was to transform the tribes of Israel into one people, to merge the different exiles and to unite the good and beautiful in each tribe and community.[3] From this perspective, beginning in the year 5716 (1956) he initiated regular visits and tours to kibbutzim, factories, development towns, and workers' councils throughout the country.[1, 2, 3] He did not appear in the kibbutzim as a "reproving prophet at the gate" chastising his listeners with rebukes, but rather conducted a cultural and respectful dialogue with them, and thereby succeeded in bringing the younger generation, which had been educated in a distinctly secular spirit, closer to the values of Jewish tradition, and in integrating traditional elements into the daily life of the kibbutz movement.[2, 3]

Rabbi Nissim worked determinedly to abolish ethnic barriers.[2] His home in Jerusalem served as a regular and unique meeting point for all segments of society: rabbis, intellectuals, politicians, judges, academics, diplomats, and community leaders from the Diaspora.[1, 2] Among the regular visitors to his home were the Kabbalah scholar Professor Gershom Scholem and Supreme Court Justice Haim Cohn.[1] These meetings created vital bridges between the world of Torah and the world of science and law, and helped to refine the fundamental problems of Israeli society through fruitful and respectful discourse.[2]

However, alongside his gentleness in drawing the distant near, Rabbi Nissim displayed absolute firmness and did not hesitate to enter the eye of the storm when he felt that the honor of tradition or of the sovereign State of Israel had been harmed. Two affairs illustrate this most clearly:

The Boycott of the Memorial for President Weizmann (1957): In November 1957, Rabbi Nissim chose to boycott the official state memorial ceremony for the first President of the State, Chaim Weizmann.[1] His decision stemmed from the fact that the ceremony was conducted in a distinctly secular format that did not conform to the tradition of Israel.[1] In this move, the Rabbi made clear that the Chief Rabbinate would not be a rubber stamp for state ceremonies emptied of traditional religious content.

The Historic Refusal to Meet Pope Paul VI (1964): During the Pope's historic visit to Israel, government officials planned for the Chief Rabbi to participate in the state reception ceremony held at Megiddo.[1, 2] Rabbi Nissim refused to come.[1, 2] He argued that since he represented the head of the sovereign Jewish religion in its land, the duty of protocol and national honor required that the Pope (as head of the Catholic religion) reciprocate with a return visit to him in Jerusalem.[1, 2] Without a guarantee of such a visit, the Rabbi explained, his participation in the reception would be interpreted as the inferiority of Judaism to Christianity, something that constituted a serious affront to the honor of the people and the state.[1, 2] His refusal aroused enormous international reverberations; the newspaper Haaretz even noted in a lead editorial that the Rabbi's decision was a historic act that granted additional validity and independence to the young State of Israel.[1, 2]

After the Six-Day War and the liberation of Jerusalem, Rabbi Nissim sought to give practical and symbolic expression to the historical connection between Hebrew law and its ancient source.[2] He moved the seat of the Chief Rabbinical Court, over which he presided as President, to a building overlooking the Southern Wall, near the Chamber of Hewn Stone where the Sanhedrin had sat in the past.[2] This was an extremely powerful symbolic move that expressed his aspiration to renew the days of the Torah judicial system as a sovereign national anchor.[2]

The "Brother and Sister" Affair and Its Implications for the Institution of the Chief Rabbinate

The early 1970s brought to the State of Israel and to the political and religious establishment one of the most severe halakhic and social crises in its history—the "Brother and Sister" affair.[4] This crisis not only undermined religion-state relations, but served as a direct political lever that led to the unprecedented dismissal of the incumbent Chief Rabbis, including Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim.[4]

The Development of the Halakhic Affair: In the 1960s, a case came before the Rabbinical Court in Petah Tikva concerning the fitness to enter the congregation of Hanokh and Miriam Langer ("brother and sister"), due to a question of mamzerut that arose concerning them.[4] The court in Petah Tikva examined the case at length, stood firmly by its opinion, and ruled that there was no avoiding defining them as mamzerim, and therefore they were forbidden to marry Jewish spouses.[4] The deliberation in the affair reached the Chief Rabbinical Court in Jerusalem.[4] Despite the heavy pressures and prolonged deliberations, the judges of the Chief Court decided not to rule on the matter themselves but to return the case to the court in Petah Tikva so that it could reexamine its decision.[4] This ruling relied on the strict halakhic principle according to which "a court does not examine another court but assumes that they are expert and will not err," which prevents hasty interference by a higher tribunal in the ruling of a local tribunal.[4]

The Political Escalation and Coalition Crisis: Since the brother and sister served at the General Staff of the IDF, near the offices of Defense Minister Moshe Dayan and the then Chief Military Rabbi Shlomo Goren, their plight became a burning national issue.[4] Defense Minister Moshe Dayan worked with all his strength to resolve the matter, and Prime Minister Golda Meir, whose heart was touched by their plight, spoke with them and demanded an institutional solution.[4] The affair dragged on for years and threatened to lead to a sharp coalition crisis between the left-wing parties (Labor-Mapam) and the National Religious Party.[4] Rabbi Shlomo Goren, while serving as Chief Military Rabbi, formulated a lenient halakhic ruling that would permit the mamzerut to be annulled, and promised Moshe Dayan that if he were elected to the position of Chief Rabbi of Israel, a special court would convene that would resolve the problem immediately.[4]

The Dismissal of the Chief Rabbis and the Historical Precedent: Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim attempted to establish a special court to re-adjudicate the affair with the aim of resolving the crisis through accepted methods, but the initiative failed due to the refusal of conservative judges to cooperate.[4] Following this failure, and in joint counsel between the Labor-Mapam party and the Mafdal party, it was decided to lead a political move to dismiss the incumbent Chief Rabbis, Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim and Rabbi Isser Yehuda Unterman, and replace them with rabbis who would be more amenable to the government and willing to resolve the crisis.[4]

On the 7th of Marcheshvan 5733 (1972), Rabbi Nissim and Rabbi Unterman were replaced by Rabbis Ovadia Yosef and Shlomo Goren (who indeed fulfilled his promise immediately after his election and permitted the brother and sister).[1, 4] This was the first time in the history of the Chief Rabbinate, since its founding by Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak HaCohen Kook, that alternative candidates were put forward for election with the aim of dismissing incumbent rabbis during their lifetimes (since until then the Chief Rabbis had been accustomed to serve for their entire lives).[1, 4]

Long-Term Effects of the Affair: The "Brother and Sister" affair and the dismissal of Rabbi Nissim had far-reaching political and religious implications for the structure of leadership in Israeli society. The affair not only changed the nature of elections to the Chief Rabbinate, but constituted a historic springboard from which new spiritual leaders in the Haredi and Religious Zionist publics emerged and became established.[5] Key figures such as Rabbi Elazar Menachem Man Shach (who in its wake became the undisputed leader of the Lithuanian-Haredi public), Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, and Rabbi Ovadia Yosef himself, established their leading positions of leadership in the wake of the crisis and turmoil that seized the institution of the Chief Rabbinate.[5]

The Written Legacy and Commemoration Projects

Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim passed away on the Ninth of Av 5741 (August 9, 1981) at the age of 85, and was buried in the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem.[1] His wife Victoria passed away several years later, in the year 57
1988.[1] He left behind a rich scholarly legacy and a unique rabbinic library that included rare manuscripts and books from early printing presses.[1, 2]

His writings and scholarly work are collected in several major compositions:

She'elot u-Teshuvot "Yein ha-Tov" (Responsa "The Good Wine") (Parts 1-2): His principal responsa work, encompassing all four parts of the Shulhan Arukh.[6, 7] The first part was first printed in 1946/1947, and the second part appeared in 1979.[6, 7] In 2006, the institution "Yad ha-Rav Nissim" issued a third and revised edition of both parts in a single volume, corrected and accompanied by a detailed source index.[7]

"Le-Dor va-Dorot" (For All Generations): A three-volume collection compiling his articles, speeches, discourses, and letters of encouragement written over the years, which appeared posthumously under the editorship of Rabbi Shemuel Katz.[1]

"Li-Khelal ve-li-Ferat - Halakhot Ketzuvot" (General and Particular - Fixed Halakhot): A three-volume series compiling his thousands of brief halakhic responses to questions from the general public and state institutions during his years of service as Chief Rabbi (edited by Rabbi Shemuel Katz).[1, 7]

Historical correspondence: Dozens of his scholarly letters were published as an appendix to the book "Yeshivot Baghdad" (Yeshivot of Baghdad), and another large collection of his correspondence with the famous Sassoon family was printed in the book "Nahalat Avot" (Patrimony of the Fathers).[1]

To perpetuate his memory and work, the institution "Yad ha-Rav Nissim" was established in the Talbiyeh neighborhood of Jerusalem, engaged in publishing his writings and in rabbinic scholarship.[7, 8] The institution published the "Sefer ha-Zikaron la-Rav Yitzhak Nissim" (Memorial Volume for Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim) in six comprehensive volumes.[8, 9] The memorial volume volumes reflect the breadth of his work and teaching:

Summary

The teaching and work of Rishon le-Tzion Rabbi Yitzhak Nissim constitute a formative chapter in shaping the spiritual character of the young State of Israel.[2] As Chief Rabbi and posek, he successfully combined uncompromising striving for authoritative halakhic truth with a warm and embracing human approach that eliminated barriers between religious and secular Jews and among the different communities.[2, 3] His firm stand on the honor of Torah and the nation—as expressed in his refusal to meet with the Pope without reciprocal conditions and in his position in the "Who is a Jew" affair—established the independent status of the Chief Rabbinate as a sovereign national institution not swayed by external pressures.[1, 2]

Although his halakhic insistence in the "Brother and Sister" affair ultimately led to his unprecedented political removal, his written and spiritual legacy continues to serve as inspiration for rabbinic leadership that combines absolute commitment to halakhah alongside broad state-oriented vision and profound love of Israel.[2, 3]
